name: ชีพจรลอยและเร็ว
preview_text: ชีพจรเต้นเร็วแบบลอยไม่ได้เป็นเพียงการเต้นของหัวใจเร็วเท่านั้น แต่ยังเป็นแผนที่: โดยจะบอกผู้ประกอบวิชาชีพ TCM ของคุณว่าความร้อนอยู่บนพื้นผิว ในปอด หรือลึกกว่านั้น และแนะนำการรักษา
categories: ["การวินิจฉัยชีพจร"]
conventional_description: Western medicine does not have a direct counterpart to the floating and rapid pulse, but a rapid heart rate (tachycardia) is often measured and can accompany fever, infection, dehydration, or stress. Standard pulse assessment focuses on rate, rhythm, and volume, but not on the depth or 'floating' quality. In TCM, the floating quality indicates that the body's defensive energy is at the surface, fighting an external pathogen - a concept not captured by conventional pulse examination.
conventional_treatments: In a conventional setting, a rapid pulse is typically viewed as a sign of fever, infection, or dehydration. Treatment focuses on the underlying cause - antibiotics for bacterial infections, antipyretics for fever, and rest. The pulse itself is not treated directly; it is monitored as a vital sign.
tcm_understanding:
In TCM, the pulse is felt at the wrist with three fingers, and the quality of the pulse reveals the state of Qi and blood in the body's organ systems. A floating pulse means that the pulse is easily felt with light pressure, as if it is bobbing at the surface. This indicates that the body's defensive Qi (Wei Qi) has rushed to the exterior to fight off an invading pathogen. A rapid pulse means the beats are faster than normal - usually over 90 per minute - which signals the presence of heat.
When these two qualities appear together, the diagnosis is clear: a heat pathogen is active in the outer layers of the body. The heat could be a wind-heat invasion caught from a change in weather, or it could be an interior heat that has pushed outward to the Lungs and skin. The exact pattern depends on the accompanying symptoms, and the same floating rapid pulse can point to four distinct pictures.
In the Wind-Heat pattern, the heat is still confined to the surface, causing mild chills, a scratchy throat, and a red-tipped tongue.
Exterior-Heat is similar but less specific - the fever may be more prominent and body aches more general. When the pathogen moves deeper, Wind-Heat invading the Lungs triggers a cough with thick yellow phlegm. Finally, Lung Heat arises when heat builds up inside the Lungs themselves, often from an unresolved infection, producing a deep cough and a pulse that still floats because the Lungs govern the skin and push the heat outward.
This is why a single Western diagnosis like 'common cold' or 'bronchitis' can have several TCM patterns. The floating rapid pulse is the starting point, but the full clinical picture - tongue, cough, phlegm, thirst - tells the practitioner exactly which formula to use.
classical_quote: 「太阴风温、温热、温疫、冬温，初起恶风寒者，桂枝汤主之；但热不恶寒而渴者，辛凉平剂银翘散主之。」
classical_translation: "When wind-warmth, warm-heat, epidemic warmth, or winter-warmth first arises with aversion to wind and cold, Gui Zhi Tang governs; if there is only heat without aversion to cold and thirst, the acrid-cool balanced formula Yin Qiao San governs. [The pulse in this presentation is typically floating and rapid.]"
classical_source:
Wen Bing Tiao Bian (Systematized Identification of Warm Diseases)  ,  Chapter 1, Upper Jiao Chapter 									·
More references
tcm_diagnosis:
A practitioner feels a floating and rapid pulse (浮数脉, fú shuò mài) by placing three fingers on the wrist. The pulse beats at the surface with little pressure, and its tempo is clearly faster than normal. This combination instantly signals that a heat pathogen is active in the body’s outer layers. The next step is to ask about chills, fever, sweating, and throat or breathing sensations, because the exact mix of these clues points toward one specific pattern.
When the pattern is Wind-Heat, the person usually reports a mild aversion to wind and a fever that feels worse than any chill. The throat is scratchy or sore, the tongue tip is red with a thin yellow coating, and a slight thirst is present. These signs confirm that the heat is still confined to the surface and has not yet moved deeper into the chest.
If the diagnosis leans toward the broader Exterior-Heat pattern, the picture is similar but often less distinct: the fever may be more prominent, the body aches more general, and the tongue appears red with a definite yellow coat. The floating rapid pulse is equally strong, but the practitioner notices fewer respiratory clues, suggesting a less localized invasion of heat at the surface.
When Wind-Heat invades the Lungs, the pulse remains floating and rapid, yet the person now describes a cough with sticky yellow phlegm, chest tightness, and a more pronounced thirst. The tongue stays red-tipped with a thin yellow coat. These respiratory signs tell the practitioner that the heat has moved beyond the skin and muscles into the Lung organ itself.
In a Lung Heat pattern, the floating rapid pulse may still appear because the Lungs govern the exterior. Here the cough is deeper, the sputum is thicker and yellower, and the fever is often higher. The tongue is red with a thicker yellow coating. Unlike the exterior patterns, chills are mild or absent, indicating that the heat is now primarily internal.

patterns.symptoms: ["Fever more pronounced than chills", "Sore, red throat", "Headache with a distending quality", "Slight sweating that does not relieve the fever", "Thirst with desire to drink", "Nasal congestion with yellow or thick discharge"]
patterns.worse_with: Exposure to wind or drafts, Spicy, fried, or greasy foods, Overexertion or overwork
patterns.better_with: Rest in a cool room, Cool fresh air, Drink plenty of fluids
patterns.why_this_happens: When Wind-Heat invades the body, it enters through the skin and mouth, lodging in the superficial layers. The body's defensive Qi rushes to the surface to fight it, making the pulse rise and feel easily palpable with light pressure - that is the 'floating' quality. The Heat pathogen accelerates the heartbeat, producing a rapid rate, so the pulse feels both floating and fast.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: red tip and edges with a thin yellow (or thin white-to-yellow) coating. Pulse: floating (felt at the surface with light pressure) and rapid (above 90 beats per minute).
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Wind-Heat is an exterior pattern, so rest allows the body to direct Qi to the surface to expel the pathogen, while fresh air and cooling fluids help clear Heat. Wind exposure drives the pathogen deeper, and spicy or heavy foods create internal Heat that compounds the exterior invasion.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Rest in a well-ventilated room, but avoid drafts. Drink plenty of lukewarm water or light herbal teas like chrysanthemum or mint. Eat light, cooling foods such as pear, mung bean soup, and watery congee; avoid spicy, greasy, or fried foods that can trap Heat.

patterns.why_this_happens: When a Heat pathogen invades from the outside, your body's defensive Qi rushes to the surface to meet it. This battle at the skin and muscle layer pushes the pulse up to the superficial level, making it feel floating. The Heat nature of the invader speeds up your circulation, giving the pulse its rapid, faster-than-normal quality.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: normal or slightly red at the tip and sides, with a thin white or faintly yellow coating. Pulse: floating (轻取即得 qīng qǔ jí dé) and rapid (数 shǔo), not tight.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Exterior Heat is a surface-level battle between your defensive Qi and a Heat pathogen. Rest and cooling measures support your body's effort to push the pathogen out, while spicy, heavy, or hot conditions add more Heat and force the pathogen deeper, making the pulse even faster and the symptoms worse.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Rest and stay hydrated with room-temperature water or mild herbal teas like chrysanthemum. Eat light, cooling foods such as pear, watermelon, and congee, and avoid spicy, greasy, or fried dishes that can trap Heat inside.

patterns.worse_with: Spicy, fried, or greasy foods, Hot, stuffy environments, Overexertion or overwork, Smoking or exposure to irritants, Stress and emotional upset
patterns.better_with: Rest in a cool room, Drink plenty of fluids, Light, bland foods (like congee or pears), Gentle deep breathing
patterns.why_this_happens: Wind-Heat invades through the nose and mouth, and because the Lung governs the exterior and opens into the nose, it is the first organ affected. The heat pathogen speeds up the circulation, making the pulse rapid, while the body's defensive Qi rushes to the surface to fight the invader, causing the pulse to float. At the same time, the Lung's ability to descend and diffuse Qi is disrupted, leading to cough and yellow phlegm.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: red tip, thin yellow coating, body slightly red. Pulse: floating (Fu) and rapid (Shu), with the right Cun position (Lung) particularly prominent.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Wind-Heat is an exterior pathogen that thrives on heat and stagnation. Resting in a cool, quiet space lets the body's defensive Qi focus on expelling the invader without adding more heat. Light, cooling foods and herbs help clear heat and resolve phlegm, while spicy, greasy foods add fuel to the fire and generate more phlegm. The Lungs are a delicate organ that needs clean, moist air to function; irritants like smoke and overexertion further disrupt their descending and diffusing action, worsening cough and sore throat.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Rest in a cool, well-ventilated room and stay hydrated with warm water or herbal teas like mint and chrysanthemum. Eat light, cooling foods such as pear, cucumber, and congee, and avoid dairy, spicy, fried, and greasy items that create phlegm and heat. Gentle deep breathing can help clear the Lungs, but avoid heavy exercise until the fever subsides.

patterns.why_this_happens:
The Lungs govern the skin and open into the nose, so they sit right at the boundary between the body's interior and the outside world. When Heat builds up deep inside the Lungs, it pushes Qi upward and outward toward the surface. This is why an interior Lung Heat pattern can make the pulse feel floating - the Heat is surging toward the exterior, even though the root of the problem is inside.
At the same time, the rapid speed of the pulse reflects the internal Heat accelerating the heartbeat. So you get a pulse that is both rapid and floating: the speed from the Heat, and the floating quality from the Lung's natural connection to the surface.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: red body, yellow dry coating, possible prickly papillae on the front third. Pulse: rapid (shu) and may feel floating; often slippery (hua) if phlegm is present, or overflowing (hong) especially at the right cun position.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Lung Heat is an interior excess Heat pattern, so anything that adds more Heat - like spicy food or smoky air - fuels the fire and makes the pulse even faster and more floating. Cooling foods and fresh air help drain the Heat and soothe the Lungs, which naturally calms the pulse. Because the Lungs govern Qi and breathing, gentle deep breathing helps restore the normal downward flow of Lung Qi, reducing the upward surge that makes the pulse feel floating at the surface.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Focus on cooling, moistening foods: pear, loquat, water chestnut, and white fungus are excellent. Avoid spicy, fried, or greasy foods that add Heat. Drink plenty of room-temperature or slightly cool water, but avoid iced drinks, which can trap the Heat. Gentle breathing exercises help the Lung Qi descend.

faqs.question: What does a floating and rapid pulse feel like?
faqs.answer: When a practitioner checks your pulse, a floating pulse is felt with only light pressure on the wrist - it seems to rise up to meet the fingers. A rapid pulse simply means the beats are faster than normal, usually over 90 per minute. Together, the pulse feels like a quick, superficial tapping that is easy to detect without pressing deeply.

faqs.question: Can I check my own floating and rapid pulse?
faqs.answer: You can get a rough idea by counting your heart rate and noticing if the pulse feels close to the skin at your wrist. However, a proper TCM pulse diagnosis requires training to distinguish subtle qualities like floating, slippery, or wiry. It’s best to have a qualified practitioner assess your pulse alongside your tongue and symptoms.

faqs.question: Does a floating rapid pulse always mean I have a fever?
faqs.answer: Not always, but it is strongly associated with heat. In many cases, a floating rapid pulse accompanies a fever or a feeling of heat. However, some people may have a rapid pulse due to anxiety or dehydration without a true fever. The presence of other signs like a sore throat, thirst, and a red-tipped tongue helps confirm the diagnosis.

faqs.question: How do herbs like Yin Qiao San help a floating rapid pulse?
faqs.answer: Yin Qiao San is a classic formula for early-stage Wind-Heat. It contains cooling, dispersing herbs like Jin Yin Hua (honeysuckle) and Lian Qiao (forsythia) that clear heat from the surface and guide the pathogen out through the skin. As the heat is released, the pulse gradually returns to a normal rate and depth. It works best when taken at the very first sign of symptoms.

faqs.question: Is it safe to exercise with a floating rapid pulse?
faqs.answer: During an active exterior invasion, your body is directing its energy to fight the pathogen. Strenuous exercise can disperse Qi and prolong recovery. Gentle activities like walking are fine if you feel up to it, but rest is the best medicine. Once the pulse normalizes and symptoms resolve, you can gradually return to your usual routine.

faqs.question: Can children have a floating rapid pulse?
faqs.answer: Yes, children often present with a floating rapid pulse when they catch a cold or flu. Their pulses are naturally a bit faster than adults', so a TCM practitioner adjusts for age. Herbal formulas can be given in reduced doses or as granules, and acupuncture points like Hegu LI-4 can be used gently. Always consult a pediatric TCM specialist.

research.title: Chinese medicinal herbs for the common cold
research.description: Cochrane systematic review evaluating the efficacy of Chinese herbal medicines, including Yin Qiao San, for the common cold. The review found some evidence of benefit but highlighted the need for larger, well-designed trials.
research.periodical: Wu T, Zhang J, Qiu Y, et al. Chinese medicinal herbs for the common cold. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews 2012, Issue 2. Art. No.: CD004782.

research.title: Effects of herbal medicines (Eunkyosan/Yin qiao san and Samsoeum) on the treatment of COVID-19: A systematic review and meta-analysis
research.description: Systematic review and meta-analysis of Yin Qiao San and related formulas for COVID-19. The study suggested these formulas may reduce time to symptom resolution and fever, but evidence quality was limited by small sample sizes.
research.periodical: Kim S, Lee H, et al. Effects of herbal medicines (Eunkyosan/Yin qiao san and Samsoeum) on the treatment of COVID-19: A systematic review and meta-analysis. PLoS One. 2023;18(7):e0288829.
